title: Claim: dict-keys-must-be-hashable
body: A dict key must be hashable. A list is not hashable, so it cannot be a key.

title: Claim: dict-preserves-insertion-order
body: dict iteration follows insertion order (a language guarantee since Python 3.7).

title: Claim: set-membership-beats-list-search
body: Testing membership in a set is far faster than a linear search of a list of the same items.

title: Claim: dict-lookup-is-constant-time
body: A dict lookup does not grow with the dict: a dict 1000 times larger costs far less than 1000 times more per lookup.

title: Complexity: dict[key] / key in dict
body:
**O(1) average**

worst case O(n) when hashes collide; rare with a good hash

title: Complexity: dict[key] = value
body:
**O(1) average**

amortized, including the occasional resize

title: Complexity: set add / remove / in
body:
**O(1) average**

a dict with no values

title: Q1: Why can a tuple be a dict key but a list cannot?
body:
A. Tuples are faster to hash
B. A tuple is immutable, so its hash cannot change; a list is mutable and not hashable
C. Lists are too large to store
D. Dicts only accept strings and tuples

**B.** A key's hash must stay fixed while the key is stored. Only immutable values can guarantee that.

title: Q2: On average, what does membership testing cost in a set of n
body:
A. O(1)
B. O(log n)
C. O(n)
D. O(n log n)

**A.** The hash picks a slot directly. Only collisions add probes, and those are rare.

title: Q3: Since Python 3.7, what does iterating over a dict return?
body:
A. Keys in sorted order
B. Keys in insertion order
C. Keys in random order
D. Keys in order of their hash

**B.** Insertion order is a language guarantee, because entries are stored in a dense array in that order.

title: Q4: Why is the 'group anagrams' problem a fit for defaultdict(li
body:
A. It sorts the words automatically
B. Each new key gets an empty list on first use, so grouping needs no existence check
C. It removes duplicate words
D. It keeps the groups sorted

**B.** defaultdict creates the missing list on access, so each word appends to its group in one step.

title: LeetCode 1: Two Sum
body:
**Pattern**: complement lookup

**Why**: Looking up target minus the current value is O(1), so one pass finds the pair.

**Python**: `dict: store each value's index, check for the complement`

title: LeetCode 49: Group Anagrams
body:
**Pattern**: group by a canonical key

**Why**: Anagrams share a key, so each word joins its group with one lookup.

**Python**: `collections.defaultdict(list), keyed by the sorted letters`

title: LeetCode 128: Longest Consecutive Sequence
body:
**Pattern**: start only at the beginning of a run

**Why**: Checking a value's neighbours is O(1), and only run starts need extending, so the total stays O(n).

**Python**: `set: membership checks`

title: Signal: Has this value been seen before, in one pass
body:
**Structure**: hash set

**Requirement**: O(1) per check

**Python**: `set`

**Example**: Two Sum (LeetCode 1): a dict of values already seen

title: Signal: Group items that share a computed key
body:
**Structure**: hash table of lists

**Requirement**: O(1) per item to find its group

**Python**: `collections.defaultdict(list)`

**Example**: Group Anagrams (LeetCode 49)

title: Signal: Find the longest run of consecutive values without sorting
body:
**Structure**: hash set

**Requirement**: O(n) total, each value checked in O(1)

**Python**: `set`

**Example**: Longest Consecutive Sequence (LeetCode 128)
